have_space_related_issues_10: I've responded to space-related issues generally by scaling down the work I do.  I live in an apartment so fabricating things out of wood is an issue; I generally use workarounds: a jigsaw instead of a table or chop saw, buying stretcher bars instead of building stretchers, asking Home Depot employees to cut down plywood so it's small enough that I can fit it into my apartment.  I worry that my neighbors will get annoyed if I'm cutting stuff too much (noise) or painting spraying too much (smell)  and I try to be courteous and keep the stuff outside my door neat (my apt complex is all single-story and I have a tiny bit of space outside of my door for two patio chairs, etc).    Some of my work is embroidery and can fit into a bag.  The work that I can do at a table or desk I often head to a cafe to do (Thunderbird Koenig has good light, big tables, and friendly staff).  I do some of my drawing and embroidery at home, too. Some artists like to work at home, most don't.  Too much distraction at home.  I think it is better to have some separation between living space and working space and I like to be around other artists working while I myself am working.      Wall space is in issue-- I don't have enough space to hang up what I'm working on to take a good look at it, or really even enough table space to lay it out.  I just deal with it and try not to get hung up on it.    I'm going to put my website here so you can see the work that I'm doing in cafes/my apartment/etc: emilyoleary.com    The fibers work is only stretched after the embroidery is completed, so while I'm working on the embroidery the whole thing can be stuffed, along with my thread and embroidery hoops, into a backpack.

have_space_related_issues_10: The biggest issue I face as an Austin artist is that I cannot afford to rent a room in this city (in a home that allows for songwriting) AND afford enough time to continue to grow/generate income from my creative practice.     In order to compose, I require a small space with lights, electricity, running water/bathroom, and Internet for booking shows bust most of all space where I can play my guitar/ sing / make noise without bothering others (somewhat soundproof).    In the past, I have worked from home... I lived in a one bedroom fourplex in San Marcos for $500 and had a piano in the space - I could keep musicians hours (writing sometimes late nights after getting home from gigs) without bothering the neighbors due to construction of the house. The neighbors were more like neighborhood than an apartment complex.    I don't know if this is possible, but it would be incredible if songwriters in the "live music capital of the world" could have city funded building full of soundproof suites to write in. With upright pianos! And after hours access! It would be like an office to work out of, so that when I'm trying to find a room to rent in this city (as close to all of the music venues as possible for as close to $500 as possible) I don't have to start my email with "I'm a musician" and try to work in halfway "I write sometimes at home, but I'm always respectful of others and can keep things quiet if need be"     The last place I rented on Manchaca, I wrote songs in my car if my roommate was asleep because the walls were too thin for even light strumming and soft singing. I've taken my guitar out of the house to parks and to sidewalks when roommates are relaxing at home to try and get those precious writing and practicing hours without being a bother. Before the rent doubled, I rented a room with another musician on Willow St. and played electric guitar a couple times- it felt so naked to be amplifying to the neighbors. But it's music. You gotta get all the kinks out somewhere. That's the art of it. And by nature, it's loud.
